questions.text: I prefer trips where I can wander freely and discover things without an itinerary.
I sense the difference between a comfortable lull in conversation and an awkward one.
I tend to share my work in progress early so others can shape it with me.
I tend to focus on whether an idea is good rather than on how it was received by the group.
When I'm excited about a future event, the excitement builds to a pitch that makes it hard to concentrate on anything else.
I consider it a compliment when people describe me as commanding.
I routinely block off calendar time that belongs exclusively to me.
I develop contingency plans for critical tasks even when things are going well.
I rarely notice when the formality of an interaction is mismatched with the actual closeness of the relationship.
The wish to respond to others' suffering is one of the strongest forces shaping my daily choices.
I notice that I can be fully engaged in a situation without my emotional volume increasing.
I account for travel time, transitions, and setup when planning my schedule.
I tend to set my thermostat, my music, and my lighting to what makes my household most comfortable, not just me.
I tend to feel emotionally prepared for whatever comes, because my system doesn't overreact.
I tend not to detect when a story is being told for the benefit of a specific listener.
I hold the view that the person most responsible for my well-being is me.
My emotional responses have a brevity to them — they arise, deliver their message, and recede.
When I'm upset, the feeling saturates my entire body.
When a friend is in real pain, I often feel little wish to relieve it.
I routinely carry extra supplies, snacks, or resources in case someone around me needs them.
I would rather make a controversial call than let the team drift without direction.
Reading or hearing about people in pain usually leaves me without much concern for them.
I routinely pick up tasks no one else wants to do, so the group can function well.
When something touches me deeply, I can feel it reverberating in my chest for hours.
I like to take time and let the group deliberate before a decision is made.
I am the first to speak up when a group needs someone to take ownership of a problem.
When I understand that someone has been hurt by unfair treatment, I care about the suffering it has caused them.
I notice when someone matches the volume of the loudest person in the room to assert themselves.
When I see someone crying, I rarely feel any wish to help.
I am the kind of person who reads the manual before using a new device.
I am content letting the group commit without needing to add my final word.
I detect when a group member's contribution is being quietly dismissed by the way others respond to it.
I start my day open to whatever feels most compelling rather than consulting a schedule.
I finalize plans late because earlier decisions might need changing anyway.
When I notice that I have overlooked someone's hardship, I become concerned about what they are experiencing.
I tend to make sure my own needs are fully met before turning my attention outward.
